"We think it was the installation or the router that was the bad actor," Duffy said in an interview with Fox News. "We're open if we see something else, we're going to continue to investigate with our federal partners and law enforcement." Duffy told ABC's "This Week" in a separate interview that the router was located in El Dorado in southern Arkansas. The equipment, along with another router that was in Amarillo, Texas, is at an L3Harris lab in Florida for examination, Duffy said. He said the router, part of ongoing work to switch from copper wire to a fiber-optic system, began flooding other systems. Federal officials said on Saturday that "instability" in communication feeds and data like radar prompted the more than four-hour ground stop. Flight disruptions lingered on Sunday but were far from the thousands of cancellations passengers faced on Friday and Saturday. There was "zero evidence" that the problem was caused by something "nefarious" or anything related to artificial intelligence, Bryan Bedford, the head of the Federal Aviation Administration, said at a press conference with Duffy Saturday morning. Bedford said no FAA facilities went dark but that officials decided to ground flights because of "instability" in information feeds to air traffic control centers that handle en route aircraft at high altitudes and eventually to others closer to airports. The issue occurred during "routine" upgrades of switching from a copper wire system to fiber, Bedford said. A router had "flooded" other routers in the air traffic control system with over 1,000 connection attempts roughly every five seconds, said Duffy. That created problems with airplane communications and radar feeds, they said. "We were unwilling to take any risk that this propagation could actually result in a center losing connectivity with aircraft," said Bedford. He said officials weren't sure for about 45 minutes what was causing the instability. The outage again thrust aging infrastructure that underpins U.S. air traffic control into the spotlight, along with the country's struggles to replace sections of it while operating the world's busiest airspace. "What we're working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error, installator error from L3 Harris, or did they install a faulty router," he said.
